entry.title: How to move your website to a new domain without losing your Google traffic
entry.summary: A step-by-step domain change: list every old URL, map each one to its new address, 301 redirect the whole domain, use Google's Change of Address tool, and know what to watch and how long to keep the old domain.
entry.content:
To move a website to a new domain without losing Google traffic, redirect every old URL to its matching new URL with a permanent (301) redirect, then tell Google with the Change of Address tool in Search Console. Keep the redirects for at least a year, keep paying for the old domain, and expect rankings to wobble for a few weeks while Google catches up.

Most traffic lost in a domain move is lost to one of three things: old pages that redirect to the homepage, old pages that redirect nowhere, or an old domain that expires. All three can be avoided. Below is the order to do it in, with what each step looks like in practice.

Before you start: change one thing

Google's own advice is to change one thing at a time. If you want a new domain, a new website builder and a new design, do them one after another, not in the same week. When traffic drops after three changes, you can't tell which one caused it.

Two more decisions to make first:

  • Pick a quiet week. Not the week before your busiest season.
  • Check your email. If your email addresses end in the old domain, they keep working only as long as the old domain's mail records do. Leave email where it is during the move. Move it later, as its own change.

Step 1: list every old URL

You can only redirect pages you know about. Build one list from several sources, because each one misses something:

  1. Your sitemap. Open olddomain.com/sitemap.xml and copy the addresses.
  2. Search Console. Open Indexing → Pages, then View data about indexed pages, and export. This is what Google actually has.
  3. Search Console Performance. Open Performance, choose the Pages tab, set the date range to 12 months and export. These are the pages that bring visitors, so they matter most.
  4. Your analytics. The landing pages report shows pages people arrive on from links, ads and old emails.
  5. Files. PDFs, menus, price lists and images that other sites link to directly.

Paste everything into one spreadsheet column and remove duplicates.

Step 2: map each old URL to one new URL

Next to each old address, write the new address that does the same job. If the paths don't change, this is easy: olddomain.com/menu becomes newdomain.com/menu. If some pages were renamed or merged, write those out one by one.

The rule: each old page goes to the closest matching new page. Not to the homepage. Google treats a pile of old pages redirected to one unrelated page as "soft 404s", which means it treats them as missing, and the traffic those pages had goes with them. If an old page has no equivalent at all, let it return 404.

When the map is done, paste it into the redirect map builder. It turns the pairs into rules for Apache, nginx, Netlify, Cloudflare and Vercel, and warns you about chains (A to B to C), loops and homepage dumps before they go live. It runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere.

Step 3: get the new site ready

Put the full site live on the new domain before you add any redirects, and check these:

  • Nothing blocks search engines. Staging sites often carry a noindex tag or a Disallow: / line in robots.txt. Open newdomain.com/robots.txt and view the source of a few pages.
  • Internal links use the new domain. Menus, footers, buttons and links inside your text. Search the site's content for the old domain name.
  • Each page's canonical tag points to itself on the new domain, not to the old one. Copied sites keep the old canonical surprisingly often.
  • A new sitemap lists the new URLs.
  • Both domains are verified in Search Console, with the same Google account, and you're an owner of both. A Domain property covers http, https, www and non-www at once. If you verify with an HTML file, copy that file to the new site too.
  • Every version of the old domain has its own property too. The Change of Address tool in step 5 runs on one host at a time: olddomain.com does not include www.olddomain.com. Add a URL-prefix property for each one, such as https://www.olddomain.com/, even the one you never used.
  • The new domain is added in Bing Webmaster Tools. Bing can import sites you've already verified in Search Console, which saves a step.

Step 4: switch on the redirects

Use server-side permanent redirects: 301 or 308. Not a JavaScript redirect, not a "this site has moved, click here" page. The redirect has to cover every version of the old domain: with and without www, http and https.

If your paths stay the same, one rule moves the whole domain and keeps the path. On nginx:

server {
    listen 80;
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name olddomain.com www.olddomain.com;
    # keep a valid certificate for the old domain here
    location / {
        return 301 https://newdomain.com$request_uri;
    }
}

On Apache, in the old site's .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^(www\.)?olddomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://newdomain.com/$1 [R=301,L]

Point the rule at the exact address your new site uses. If the new site lives on www.newdomain.com, write that, or every old link takes two hops instead of one.

If some paths changed, you need the page-by-page rules from your map as well, and they have to win over the whole-domain rule:

  • nginx: add them as location = /old-path blocks in the same server block. An exact match beats location / wherever it sits. That's why the example wraps its return in location /: a return written directly in the server block runs before nginx looks at any location, so the page rules would never fire (nginx's rewrite module docs give the order).
  • Apache: put them above the whole-domain rule. RewriteRule lines run top to bottom. Redirect and RedirectMatch lines in .htaccess run before any RewriteRule, wherever they sit (Apache's docs), so those win too.

One thing people miss: the old domain still needs a valid HTTPS certificate. Every old link starts with https://olddomain.com. If the certificate has lapsed, the browser shows a security warning before the redirect ever runs, and most visitors leave.

Test every row, not three

Save your map as a text file, one pair per line, old and new separated by a space. Then run this in a terminal (Mac and Linux have curl built in):

while read -r old new || [ -n "$old" ]; do
  got=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}' "$old")
  [ "$got" = "301 $new" ] || echo "WRONG $old -> $got (want 301 $new)"
done < map.txt

It prints nothing when every row is right. Each line it prints is a page to fix. If you used 308 redirects, change 301 to 308 in the third line.

If every row prints WRONG even though the redirects work in a browser, check how the file was saved. A file saved from Excel or on Windows ends its lines with an invisible carriage return, so the expected address never matches. Strip it with tr -d '\r' < map.txt > map-clean.txt and run the loop on map-clean.txt.

Then check that the new addresses themselves load, without a second redirect:

while read -r old new || [ -n "$old" ]; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$new")
  [ "$code" = "200" ] || echo "$code $new"
done < map.txt

On Windows, open PowerShell. Windows 10 and 11 include curl.exe, so the same two checks are:

Get-Content map.txt | ForEach-Object {
  $old, $new = $_ -split ' '
  $got = curl.exe -s -o NUL -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}' $old
  if ($got -ne "301 $new") { "WRONG $old -> $got (want 301 $new)" }
}

Get-Content map.txt | ForEach-Object {
  $old, $new = $_ -split ' '
  $code = curl.exe -s -o NUL -w '%{http_code}' $new
  if ($code -ne '200') { "$code $new" }
}

For a single page, Search Console's URL Inspection tool does the same check from Google's side.

Step 5: tell Google and Bing

In Search Console, open the old domain's property, go to Settings → Change of address, and pick the new domain. The tool checks that you own both sites and that a few old pages return 301s, then asks Google to crawl the new site first and carry signals across. It works only for real domain or subdomain changes, not for moving from http to https or from www to non-www.

Run it once for every version of the old domain: from olddomain.com, then again from www.olddomain.com, both to the new domain. Google's guide says to do this for all variants, even the ones you don't use. One request covers both http and https of the same host.

Then open the new domain's property and submit the new sitemap under Indexing → Sitemaps.

Bing used to have a Site Move tool. It's gone from the current Bing Webmaster Tools, and Microsoft's answer is that 301 redirects are enough. Submit the new sitemap in Bing Webmaster Tools, and use Submit URLs (Bing help) for your ten most important pages so they're crawled first. Bing matters beyond Bing: Microsoft Copilot searches with it.

Step 6: change the address everywhere else

Redirects catch old links, but every link still costs a hop. Update the ones you control:

  • your Google Business Profile and Bing Places website field;
  • social media profiles and link-in-bio pages;
  • directory listings, marketplaces and review sites;
  • ads, QR codes you're about to print, email signatures and invoice templates;
  • payment, booking and newsletter tools that store your website address.

If a few sites link to you a lot, ask them to update the link. That's the one request in this list worth sending.

Step 7: watch, and keep the old domain

Google says a small to medium site takes a few weeks for most pages to move, and larger sites longer. Rankings may go up and down in that time. That's normal. A steady fall after a month is not, and usually means a redirect problem: run the test from step 4 again.

What to look at, once a week:

  • Pages report, both properties. Indexed pages on the old domain should go down, and on the new domain go up.
  • Performance report, new property. Clicks and impressions should climb as the old property's fall.
  • Pages report, "Not found (404)". Old URLs you forgot to map show up here. Add them to the map.

How long to keep the redirects: Google's site-move guide says at least a year, and suggests keeping them for good. The Change of Address request itself lasts 180 days, so treat 180 days as the floor, not the finish. Old links in emails, forums and bookmarks never stop working on their own schedule.

Keep the old domain. Google recommends paying for it for at least a year, so nobody else buys it and uses your old reputation. Domains cost little to renew. Set it to auto-renew and keep it as long as anything still links to it.

Mistakes that cost traffic

  • Redirecting every old page to the new homepage. Google treats them as missing pages.
  • Temporary (302) redirects. They tell search engines the old address is coming back.
  • Redirect chains. Old domain to new http to new https to new www: four hops. Send each old URL straight to its final address.
  • Blocking the old domain in robots.txt. Google then can't crawl the old pages, so it never sees the redirects.
  • Letting the old certificate or the old domain lapse. Every old link breaks at once.
  • Moving domain, design and platform in one go. If traffic falls, you won't know why.

The checklist

  1. Leave email and design alone; change only the domain.
  2. List every old URL: sitemap, Search Console exports, analytics, files.
  3. Map each old URL to its closest new URL. No homepage dumps.
  4. Put the new site live: no noindex, new internal links, self canonicals, new sitemap.
  5. Verify both domains in Search Console, plus a property for each old variant, and add the new one to Bing.
  6. Switch on 301s for every version of the old domain. Keep its certificate valid.
  7. Test every row of the map with curl.
  8. Run Change of Address in Search Console, once for each old variant (www and non-www). Submit the new sitemap to Google and Bing.
  9. Update your business profiles, social profiles, listings and print.
  10. Check the Pages and Performance reports weekly for a couple of months.
  11. Keep the redirects and the old domain for at least a year. Longer is better.

Sources: Google's site move with URL changes guide, Google's Change of Address tool help page, and Microsoft's answer on the retired Bing Site Move tool. If you're also cleaning up pages you don't need any more, here's how to find and retire old pages.

entry.title: How to check what ChatGPT and Google's AI say about your business, and fix a wrong answer
entry.summary: Ask the assistants the questions your customers ask, open the sources behind each answer, and fix the page the wrong fact came from. A 30-minute check for small businesses, with a table to fill in.
entry.content:
To check what an AI assistant says about your business, ask it the questions your customers ask, in a new chat, and write down the answers. When one is wrong, open the sources the assistant shows under the answer. The wrong fact almost always sits on one of those pages. Fix that page, then check again in a week or two.

It takes about 30 minutes. Here is how to do it step by step.

Step 1: ask what your customers ask

Use the list of questions people ask you on the phone and at the counter. If you don't have one yet, this post on what to put on your website starts with it.

Ask each question two ways:

  • By name: "Is Example Bakery open on Sunday?" "Does Example Bakery deliver?" This shows what the assistant knows about you.
  • By need: "Where can I order a birthday cake for delivery in [your city]?" This shows whether you come up at all when someone doesn't know your name yet.

Ask in more than one place. Your customers use different ones:

  • ChatGPT, with search turned on, so it reads the web instead of answering from memory. If it doesn't search on its own, select View all tools, then Search, before you ask, or type / in the message box and pick Search (OpenAI help).
  • Google: a normal search that shows an AI Overview, and AI Mode.
  • Microsoft Copilot, which answers from Bing.
  • Any other assistant your customers mention, such as Gemini, Claude or Perplexity.

Start a new chat for each question. A chat remembers what you said earlier in it, and you want the answer a stranger would get.

If you'd rather not write the questions yourself, this free check builds them from your business name, what you sell and your town, keeps score of the answers, and checks the robots.txt you paste into it for the bots that matter (a browser page can't fetch it from your site, so you copy it in).

Step 2: write the answers down

Answers change from week to week, so keep a record. A simple table is enough:

Date   | Assistant | Question            | Answer said     | Right? | Source it showed
------ | --------- | ------------------- | --------------- | ------ | ----------------
10 Oct | ChatGPT   | Open on Sunday?     | "Closed Sunday" | Wrong  | old directory listing
10 Oct | Google AI | Do you deliver?     | "Yes, citywide" | Right  | yourdomain.com/faq
10 Oct | Copilot   | Birthday cake, city | not mentioned   | Missing| -

Mark each answer one of four ways:

  • Right. Nothing to do.
  • Wrong. A fact that isn't true: old hours, a closed branch, a price from two years ago.
  • Hedged. "Hours may vary, check their website." Usually the sources disagree, or none states the fact plainly.
  • Missing. You don't come up, or it says it can't find you.

Step 3: trace each wrong answer to its source

This is the step most people skip. The assistant didn't invent your old hours from nothing. It read them somewhere.

Where to find the sources:

  • ChatGPT: answers that used search show small citation links in the text, and a Sources button at the end of the answer that opens the full list (OpenAI help). OpenAI's own help page says citations can be incomplete, outdated or wrong, and tells you to open the source and check it supports the answer. That is this step.
  • Google AI Overviews and AI Mode: the overview shows links "to supporting information from the web" next to the text (Google help).
  • Copilot and most other assistants show numbered links in or under the answer.

Open each source and search the page for the wrong fact (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F). The usual culprits:

  1. An old page on your own site. A 2023 price list, a "holiday hours" post nobody removed, a page for a branch that closed. It's still indexed, so it's still read.
  2. Your Google Business Profile or Bing Places listing with hours you never updated.
  3. A directory or review site that copied your details years ago.
  4. A social media page with an old bio or a pinned post.

If the answer shows no source at all, it probably came from what the model learned in training, not from a search. Ask the same question again and add "search the web". If the searched answer is right, the web is fine and the old answer will fade as models are updated. You can't speed that part up.

Don't trust the assistant if you ask it "where did you get that?" It may name a page it never read. Only the links it shows count, and only after you open them and find the fact there.

Step 4: fix the page, not the answer

Match each culprit to its fix:

  • Old page on your site: update it with the current facts. If it shouldn't exist, delete it, or redirect its address to the current page so old links still land somewhere useful. How to find old pages and remove them properly.
  • Business profile: edit it in Google Business Profile or Bing Places. Use exactly the hours and address your website shows.
  • Directory or review site: most let owners claim a listing and edit it. If not, look for a "suggest an edit" or contact link.
  • Hedged answers: look for two sources that disagree, and make them agree. If no source states the fact plainly, write it as one plain sentence on your own site: "We are open Sunday, 9:00 to 14:00."
  • Missing answers: check that your site is in search at all. Search site:yourdomain.com on Google and Bing, or use this checklist builder, then read how to check that Google can see your site.

Arguing with the assistant inside your own chat doesn't fix anything for anyone else. As far as I know, a correction you type into a chat changes that chat, not the answer a stranger gets tomorrow.

Step 5: tell the search engines, then report

After you fix a page on your site, ask the search engines to read it again. Assistants that search can't see the fix until then.

  1. In Google Search Console, paste the page's address into the search bar at the top (URL Inspection) and click Request indexing.
  2. In Bing Webmaster Tools, open Submit URLs, paste the page's address (one per line) and click Submit (Bing help). If your site or host supports IndexNow, it tells Bing and other engines for you.

Then report the answer itself. On a Google AI Overview, click the thumbs-down icon at the bottom, then "Report a problem", choose a category and add a sentence in the text field (Google help). In ChatGPT, use the thumbs-down under the answer. I don't know how much these reports change future answers; Google and OpenAI don't say. They take ten seconds, so do them, but the page fix is the part that works.

Step 6: check again

Put a reminder in your calendar for one to two weeks later. Ask the same questions in the same assistants and add a new row to your table for each. I can't tell you how long a fix takes to show up: it depends on when the page is next crawled and which source the assistant picks that day. The table tells you.

After that, repeat the whole check once a month, and every time something changes: new hours, a move, new prices, a branch opening or closing.

What I learned

The useful question isn't "what does the AI think of us?" It's "which page did it read?" An answer is a copy of pages. When the copy is wrong, there's an original to fix, and that original is usually something you or a directory published years ago and forgot.

So the cleanup that helps most is boring: find your old pages and listings, and make every one of them say the same thing as your website today.

The checklist

  1. Ask each customer question by name and by need, in a new chat.
  2. Ask ChatGPT (with search), Google (AI Overview and AI Mode) and Copilot.
  3. Write each answer in a table: right, wrong, hedged or missing, plus its sources.
  4. Open the sources of every wrong answer and find the page with the wrong fact.
  5. Fix that page, profile or listing. Make all of them match your website.
  6. Request indexing in Search Console and use Submit URLs in Bing Webmaster Tools.
  7. Report the wrong answer with the thumbs-down.
  8. Check again in one to two weeks, then monthly.

entry.title: How to find old pages of your website that still show up in Google, and remove them properly
entry.summary: Old price lists, closed branches and expired offers stay in Google and get read by AI assistants. How to find them with site: and before:, decide update, redirect or delete, and make the removal stick.
entry.content:
To find old pages that still show up in Google, search site:yourdomain.com with words like "price", "hours" or a past year, and export the indexed pages from Google Search Console. For each old page, update it, redirect it to the page that replaced it, or delete it so it returns a 404. Then use Google's Removals tool to hide it while Google catches up.

Old pages matter more than they used to. Search engines show them, and AI assistants that search the web read them and repeat what they say. If ChatGPT quotes your 2023 prices, there's usually a 2023 page behind it. This post is the cleanup that follows checking what assistants say about you.

Step 1: find the old pages

Use more than one way. Each one finds pages the others miss.

Search Google with operators

Type these into Google, with your own domain:

site:yourdomain.com price
site:yourdomain.com hours
site:yourdomain.com 2023
site:yourdomain.com offer OR promotion OR holiday
site:yourdomain.com before:2024

before: finds pages last updated before a date, and takes a year or a full date like before:2024-06-01. Google documents it on its Refine searches page, along with site:, - and after:. The date is Google's idea of when the page changed, so treat it as a hint, not a fact.

To look at one stretch of time, combine the two: site:yourdomain.com after:2021-01-01 before:2023-01-01 shows pages Google thinks were last updated in 2021 or 2022. That's handy when you know roughly when the old prices or the old address were on the site.

Search for the things that go out of date: prices, hours, addresses, branch names, staff pages, menus, events, job ads, and the names of products you no longer sell.

Export the list from Search Console

  1. In Google Search Console, open Indexing → Pages.
  2. Click View data about indexed pages.
  3. Click Export and open the file in a spreadsheet.

The table stops at 1,000 rows (source). Most small sites fit. Read the addresses top to bottom. Old pages give themselves away by their paths: /2022-menu, /summer-sale, /branch-old-street.

Do the same in Bing Webmaster Tools. Bing feeds Microsoft Copilot, and its index is not a copy of Google's.

Check what still gets visits

Before you delete anything, open Search Console's Performance report, click Pages, and look up each old page. A page that still gets clicks has people arriving on it. It needs a redirect, not a dead end.

Step 2: decide what each page becomes

Every old page gets one of four outcomes. Write it in a new column next to the address.

  • Update when the page is still useful but some facts changed. Fix the facts, keep the address. This keeps any links pointing to it.
  • Redirect when a newer page does the same job: the 2023 price list becomes the current price list, the closed branch points to the nearest open one. Use a permanent redirect (301 or 308). Google treats it as a strong signal that the new page should take the old one's place (source). With more than a handful, list them in two columns and paste them into the redirect map builder: it writes the rules for Apache, nginx, Netlify, Cloudflare or Vercel and catches chains and loops.
  • Delete when nothing replaced it: an expired offer, an event that happened, a product you'll never sell again. The server must answer with a 404 or 410 status.
  • Noindex when some people still need the page but searchers shouldn't land on it, like an old terms-and-conditions page that existing customers signed. Add <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> to its <head>. Old price lists are often PDFs, which have no <head>. For those, the server sends the header X-Robots-Tag: noindex instead (Google and Bing both read it). Or just delete the PDF.

404 or 410 doesn't matter much. Google says it treats all 4xx codes except 429 the same way: the page is dropped from the index if it was there (source). Pick whichever your website builder makes easy.

Step 3: check that it actually worked

Website builders get this wrong more often than you'd think. A "deleted" page can still answer with a 200 status and a friendly "page not found" message. Google calls that a soft 404, and it stays a problem (source).

Check each changed address. In a terminal, on Mac or Linux:

curl -sI https://yourdomain.com/summer-sale | head -1
# HTTP/2 404              deleted, good
# HTTP/2 301              redirected, good
# HTTP/2 200              still there: not done

Type the address exactly as Google lists it, usually with https://. A 301 can also just mean "use https" or "add www". So for any redirect, also check where it goes:

curl -sIL https://yourdomain.com/2023-prices | grep -i '^location'

If the last location is the same page on https:// or www, run the first command again on that address. Its status is the one that counts.

On Windows, PowerShell has curl.exe built in but no head or grep. Use these instead:

curl.exe -sI https://yourdomain.com/summer-sale | Select-Object -First 1
curl.exe -sIL https://yourdomain.com/2023-prices | Select-String '^location'

No terminal? Use Search Console's URL Inspection: paste the address in the bar at the top, then click Test live URL. It shows what Google gets back right now.

Step 4: hide it now, while Google catches up

Google drops a deleted page only when it crawls that address again. That can take weeks for a page nobody links to. If the old page is doing harm, like quoting a wrong price, hide it in the meantime:

  • Google: Search Console → Indexing → Removals → New request. This hides the page from search for about six months. It does not delete it. Google's own words: the tool "provides only a temporary removal" (source). The 404, redirect or noindex from step 2 is what makes it permanent.
  • Bing: Bing Webmaster Tools' Block URLs. Also temporary; a block lasts 90 days unless you extend it. Bing's page on removing a page from Bing or Copilot for good lists the same permanent fixes: a 404 or 410, or noindex.

If you already use IndexNow, submit the changed and deleted addresses there too. It tells Bing and other engines that use it to look again.

When the old page isn't yours

Sometimes the old fact sits on someone else's site: a directory, a news article, a blog. If that page is gone or has already been fixed but the old version still shows in search, anyone can ask for a refresh:

  • Google: the Refresh Outdated Content tool.
  • Bing: the Content Removal tool.

If the page is live and still wrong, these tools can't help. Ask the site to update it. Most directories let owners claim and edit their listing.

Mistakes to skip

  • Blocking old pages in robots.txt. It feels like removal. It isn't. If Google can't fetch the page, it never sees the noindex, and "the page can still appear in search results" (source). Let the crawler in so it can read the 404 or the noindex. To see whether a line in your robots.txt still blocks a page, paste the file and the address into the robots.txt tester.
  • Redirecting everything to the home page. It's one rule instead of twenty, and it helps nobody. Someone who clicked "2023 price list" wants prices, not your welcome banner. Redirect each page to its closest match, and delete the ones that have none.
  • Using a temporary redirect. 302 and 307 tell Google the move might be undone, so it may keep showing the old address. Use 301 or 308 for pages that are gone for good.
  • Panicking at the 404 count. After a cleanup, Search Console's Not found (404) list grows. For pages you deleted on purpose, that is the report doing its job, not an error to fix.
  • Forgetting the links. Search your own site for links to the pages you removed and change them. Your menus and old blog posts are often the reason a dead page keeps getting crawled.

The checklist

  1. Search site:yourdomain.com with "price", "hours", past years, and before:.
  2. Export indexed pages from Search Console (and Bing Webmaster Tools) into a spreadsheet.
  3. Look up each old page in the Performance report before you touch it.
  4. Mark each one: update, redirect (301), delete (404/410) or noindex.
  5. Make the change, then check the status code with curl -sI or URL Inspection.
  6. Hide harmful pages with Google's Removals tool and Bing's Block URLs while you wait.
  7. Fix your own links to removed pages.
  8. Search site: again in a few weeks, and repeat once a year.

entry.title: What to put on your business website so ChatGPT and Google can answer questions about it
entry.summary: AI assistants answer from pages that web search finds. Put your hours, location, prices and how to order as plain text on an indexed page, keep the facts the same everywhere, and skip the "AI SEO" extras. A checklist for small businesses.
entry.content:
To let ChatGPT, Google's AI answers and other assistants answer questions about your business, put the facts people ask about as plain text on your website: what you sell, where you are, when you're open, what it costs, and how to order. Make sure search engines have indexed that page. Keep the same facts on your Google Business Profile.

That's most of it. No special file or markup is required. This post shows what to write, where to put it, and what to skip.

Where an assistant gets its answer

When someone asks an assistant about a business, it usually runs a web search, reads a few of the pages it finds, and writes an answer from them. If your page isn't in the search results, the assistant can't read it.

Google says so directly about its AI Overviews and AI Mode: "There are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode." A page must be "indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet" (source).

ChatGPT's search uses its own crawler, OAI-SearchBot. OpenAI's docs say sites that block it "will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers" (source).

Step 1: list the questions people actually ask

Write down the questions customers ask you on the phone, in messages and at the counter. For most small businesses they are some of these:

  • Are you open now? On Sunday? On holidays?
  • Where are you, and is there parking?
  • Do you deliver to my area? How long does it take, and what does it cost?
  • How much is it? Is there a minimum order?
  • Do you have this item, size or service?
  • How do I order or book? Can I pay by card, or cash on delivery?
  • How do I reach you?

Each answer you write down is a sentence that belongs on your website. Use the words customers use. "Do you deliver?" is what people type. "Logistics solutions" is not.

Step 2: put each answer in text, where it's easy to find

  • The first lines of your home page say what you are and where: "A bakery selling bread and cakes, with delivery across the city." One plain sentence. Assistants and search snippets both read the top of the page first.
  • Hours and address as text, on the home page or a contact page. Say which days you're closed, in words: "Closed on Sundays." Add holiday changes when they happen, and take them down after.
  • Prices on a page, even if only "from" prices or ranges. "Call for prices" gives an assistant nothing to repeat.
  • A short FAQ page with the questions from step 1 as headings and one or two sentences under each.

Things that hide your facts:

  • Opening hours only in an image, a poster photo or an Instagram post.
  • A menu or price list only as a PDF or a photo.
  • Facts that only appear after a click, inside a pop-up or a chat widget.

Images are fine. Just write the same facts as text next to them. Google's own advice for its AI features is to make sure "important content is available in textual form" (source).

Step 3: keep the facts the same everywhere

An assistant may read your website, your Google Business Profile, your Facebook page and a directory listing in one answer. If your website says you close at 6 and your profile says 8, it has to pick one, or hedge.

Google's help for Business Profiles says: "If your business info isn't accurate, your Business Profile might not show up for relevant searches in your area" (source). It also asks for complete info: address, hours, category, and attributes like parking. Its list of practices for AI features includes "Checking that your Merchant Center and Business Profile information is up-to-date."

For holidays, use the profile's Special hours instead of changing your regular hours. It covers short changes and closures of up to 6 days in a row, and Google suggests confirming your hours for official holidays even when they don't change (source).

Pick one place as the source of truth, usually your website. When something changes, update it there first, then the profile, then the rest. Bing has its own listing too, Bing Places, and Microsoft's assistant answers from Bing.

Step 4: check that search engines can read the page

  1. Search site:yourdomain.com on Google and on Bing. If your pages don't show up, start with checking that Google can see your site. This checklist builder fills in the links for your domain.
  2. Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt. Make sure it doesn't block Googlebot, Bingbot or OAI-SearchBot. A line like Disallow: / under User-agent: * blocks all of them. To see which line decides it for a given page and bot, paste the file into this robots.txt tester.
  3. If you, or your website builder, added AI-crawler blocks, read them line by line. OpenAI lists separate crawlers for search and for model training, each with its own robots.txt name. Block the one you mean, not both by accident.
  4. Check your host or CDN too. Google's list says crawling must be allowed "in robots.txt, and by any CDN or hosting infrastructure." A firewall can turn a bot away before it ever reads robots.txt. On Cloudflare, look under Security Settings, Configure AI bot policies. It sorts AI bots into Search, Agent and Training, and each can be blocked everywhere, blocked on pages with ads, or allowed. Search crawlers are the ones that let an assistant find you later. Agent covers bots that fetch your page in real time when someone asks an assistant about it. Crawlers that do both search and training count as Training there (source).

A robots.txt that lets everyone in looks like this:

User-agent: *
Allow: /

Sitemap: https://yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml

Optional: describe the business in structured data

Structured data is a small block of code that states your facts in a fixed format. Google says no special structured data is needed for its AI features. It still uses LocalBusiness data for regular search results, and it's a cheap way to state your hours without ambiguity.

Put this in the <head> of your home page, with your own values:

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Bakery",
  "name": "Example Bakery",
  "url": "https://yourdomain.com/",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "1 Example Street",
    "addressLocality": "Your City",
    "addressCountry": "XX"
  },
  "openingHoursSpecification": [{
    "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
    "dayOfWeek": ["Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday","Saturday"],
    "opens": "08:00",
    "closes": "19:00"
  }],
  "priceRange": "$$"
}
</script>

Two rules. Use the most specific type that fits (Bakery, Restaurant, Dentist; schema.org lists them). And every value must match what the page itself says. Data that disagrees with the visible text is worse than none. If you'd rather not type the code by hand, this free builder writes it from a form, hours included, and gives you a matching hours list for the page.

Hours trip people up most. The example lists Monday to Saturday only. To say plainly that you're closed on Sunday, Google's docs say to add a Sunday entry with both opens and closes set to "00:00". Open around the clock is "00:00" to "23:59". Holiday closures get their own entry with validFrom and validThrough dates (source):

{
  "@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
  "dayOfWeek": "Sunday",
  "opens": "00:00",
  "closes": "00:00"
}

Before you publish, paste the page URL or the code into Google's Rich Results Test. It shows whether the block parses and which fields Google read.

What doesn't matter

  • llms.txt files. Google says you don't need "new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. On the sites I work on, we found no evidence that any assistant read one.
  • Writing for robots. Repeating "best bakery near me" ten times doesn't help. One clear sentence that answers the question does.
  • Paid "AI SEO" packages that promise placement in ChatGPT. Nobody can sell a place in an assistant's answer. The work is the four steps above.

What I learned

On a directory site I work on, the first visitors from ChatGPT arrived within days of launch. The pages they landed on had one thing in common: the first lines answered one specific question, with the name, the place and the facts. The general pages got nothing.

So write the answer first. Explain later, if at all.

The checklist

  1. List the questions customers ask you.
  2. Say what you are and where in the first line of your home page.
  3. Put hours, address, prices and how to order as text, not only in images or PDFs.
  4. Add a short FAQ with those questions as headings.
  5. Make your website, Google Business Profile and Bing Places say the same thing.
  6. Check site: on Google and Bing, read your robots.txt, and check your host's AI-bot settings.
  7. Optional: add LocalBusiness structured data that matches the page, and test it.
  8. Ask an assistant about your business. If the answer is wrong, find which page it came from and fix that page. Here's how to do that check.

entry.title: How to test a checkout automation without placing a real order
entry.summary: A script that buys things online needs a dry run that can't spend money. Don't trust button labels. Block the order request in the browser itself. Here are the steps, with code.
entry.content:
If you automate a checkout, you have to test it on the real store. Test shops don't have the real store's cookie banners, bot checks, address forms or surprise upsell pages.

But a test on the real store can place a real order. Someone gets charged. A parcel gets packed. A shop owner deals with a cancellation that was your fault.

The answer is a dry run that can't place an order even when your script is wrong. Here is how I build one.

1. Don't decide by button labels

The obvious dry run is "click everything except the final button". It fails because you don't know which button is final.

  • On one store the last button says Place order. On another it says Continue, and that Continue places the order.
  • Some stores skip the review page when you're signed in or paying cash on delivery. The step you planned to stop at never appears.
  • Labels change with language, A/B tests and redesigns. A script that worked last month can click straight through today.

So the label check can stay, as a first fence. It can't be the only one.

2. Block the order request in the browser

An order is not a click. It's a network request: usually a POST to a path with words like checkout, order, payment or complete in it. If that request never leaves the browser, no order exists, whatever your script clicked.

Browser automation tools let you intercept every request. In Playwright it looks like this:

const DRY_RUN = process.env.DRY_RUN !== "0";
const ORDER_WORDS = /(checkout|order|payment|purchase|complete|confirm)/i;

// Service workers can send requests the filter never sees; turn them off.
const context = await browser.newContext({ serviceWorkers: "block" });

if (DRY_RUN) {
  // context.route, not page.route: it also covers popups and new tabs.
  await context.route("**/*", (route) => {
    const req = route.request();
    const writes = req.method() !== "GET" && req.method() !== "HEAD";
    if (writes && ORDER_WORDS.test(req.url())) {
      console.log("DRY RUN blocked:", req.method(), req.url());
      return route.abort();
    }
    return route.continue();
  });
}

const page = await context.newPage();

Puppeteer does the same with page.setRequestInterception(true) and request.abort().

Two lines in there are easy to miss. Payment steps often open in a popup or a new tab, and a filter set on one page doesn't follow them; a filter on the whole browser context does. And a store's service worker can send requests your filter never sees, so Playwright's docs say to block service workers when you intercept requests.

Three details matter more than the code:

  1. Dry run is the default. The variable has to be set on purpose to go live. A forgotten flag should mean "safe", not "spend".
  2. Block too much, then loosen. The pattern above also blocks some harmless requests, like adding to cart on stores whose cart path says order. That's fine. Watch the log, and allow specific paths one by one.
  3. Log every block. The log tells you where the store's order request actually goes. That's the most useful thing a dry run teaches you.

3. Pay with something that can't pay

Add a second, independent fence. If a store offers cash on delivery, choose it in tests: no card number exists to charge. If you must test a card form, use a card that will decline, and never one tied to real money.

Two fences that fail in different ways are far safer than one clever fence.

4. Check the cart before checkout, every time

The mistake I didn't expect wasn't the final click. It was the cart.

Stores remember carts. Run a test twice in the same session and the second run starts with the first run's items still there. Some stores also add one item twice when your script's click registers as two.

So before the script enters checkout, it reads the cart and compares it to what it meant to buy: same items, same sizes, same count. If anything differs, it stops. It doesn't try to fix the cart; it stops and says why.

5. Untick what you didn't choose

Checkout forms come with boxes already ticked: newsletters, marketing texts, "save my details", sometimes a paid add-on like gift wrap or insurance. A person would notice them. A script won't, unless you tell it to.

Before the last step, have the script find every checked checkbox on the page and log it. Untick everything that isn't required. Fail the run if a required box is one you don't recognise.

6. Record once, replay many times

Every run against a live store costs something: rate limits, bot checks, and the chance of a mistake. Once a dry run passes, save the pages and responses it saw. Playwright can record traffic to a HAR file and replay it.

Then test your edge cases offline: an item that sold out between cart and checkout, a missing size, a cart that came back with an extra item. You can stage those in a saved copy. On the live store you'd have to wait for them to happen.

What didn't work

  • Stopping on a page title. "Stop when the page says Review your order" broke on the first store that had no review page.
  • Running from a server. Some large stores refuse traffic from data-centre connections outright. No amount of waiting gets past that. If a store blocks you, accept it; working around a store's bot protection isn't testing anymore.
  • One fence. Every single safeguard I tried had a store where it didn't apply. Only stacking them held.

The checklist

  1. Dry run is the default; going live needs a deliberate switch.
  2. Order-placing requests are blocked in the browser, popups and new tabs included, with service workers off, and every block is logged.
  3. Tests pay with a method that can't charge anyone.
  4. The cart is checked against the intended items before checkout.
  5. Pre-ticked boxes are found, logged and unticked.
  6. Edge cases are replayed offline, not waited for live.

None of this is specific to shopping. Any script that sends an email, books a slot or moves money needs the same thing: a dry run the code can't talk its way out of.

entry.title: How to tell if your website visitors are bots, and filter them out of Google Analytics 4
entry.summary: GA4 removes known bots, but not headless browsers run from cloud servers. Here are the fingerprints to look for, a five-minute check, and a safe way to filter them with a data filter you test first.
entry.content:
If Google Analytics 4 shows visitors who all view one page, stay zero seconds, use the same odd screen size and come from a city where you have no customers, they are probably bots.

GA4 already removes known bots. It does not remove all of them. This post shows how to spot the rest, and how to filter them without losing real data by mistake.

Why GA4 still counts some bots

Google says GA4 excludes "traffic from known bots and spiders" automatically, using its own research and the IAB's International Spiders and Bots List. You can't turn this off, and you can't see how much it removed (source).

That list works on bots that say who they are. It misses scripts that drive a real browser, like headless Chrome, from a rented cloud server. They load your page, run your JavaScript, and fire the GA4 tag like any visitor.

Small and new sites feel this most. A site with 20 real visitors a week and 200 automated ones shows a picture that is 90% wrong.

The fingerprints

No single sign proves a bot. Look for several at once, on the same group of sessions:

  • One screen size, repeated. 800 × 600 is the one I saw most. It's the default window of headless Chrome and the default viewport in Puppeteer. Few real people browse at that size today.
  • Cities that host cloud data centres, not cities where your customers live. If you sell in one country and a third of your users are in a single town in another, open that town's row.
  • One page, zero engagement. Views per session of 1, average engagement time near 0 seconds, and almost no engaged sessions.
  • Direct traffic. No referrer, no search, no campaign. Bots rarely arrive from a link.
  • Bursts. Many sessions in the same hour, then none.

A five-minute check

  1. In GA4, open Explore and start a Free form exploration.
  2. Add the dimensions City, Screen resolution and Session default channel group.
  3. Add the metrics Sessions, Engaged sessions and Average engagement time per session.
  4. Put Screen resolution and City in rows. Sort by Sessions.
  5. Read the top rows. A row with many sessions, almost no engaged sessions and near-zero time is your suspect.

If the suspects are a small share, you can stop here and just keep them in mind. If they are most of your traffic, filter them.

Filter them: tag first, drop later

GA4 data filters are permanent. Google's words: "the excluded data is never processed and will never be available" (source). They also don't apply to the past. So don't start by deleting. Start by labelling.

GA4's internal-traffic filter matches an event parameter called traffic_type. Usually an IP rule sets it. You can also set it yourself, from your own page, with any rule you like. That's the trick.

Step 1: label suspected bots in your tag

Change your GA4 snippet so it marks sessions that look automated:

<script>
  window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
  function gtag(){dataLayer.push(arguments);}
  gtag('js', new Date());

  var looksAutomated =
    navigator.webdriver === true ||
    /HeadlessChrome|PhantomJS/i.test(navigator.userAgent) ||
    (screen.width === 800 && screen.height === 600);

  if (looksAutomated) gtag('set', { traffic_type: 'bot' });

  gtag('config', 'G-XXXXXXXXXX');
</script>

navigator.webdriver is true in browsers controlled by automation tools, as the WebDriver standard requires. The user-agent test catches headless Chrome that doesn't hide itself. The screen test catches the default window size. Change the rule to match what your own check found.

This only sees bots that run JavaScript. That's fine: those are the only bots GA4 can see too.

Step 2: create the filter in Testing

  1. Go to Admin → Data collection and modification → Data filters → Create filter.
  2. Choose Internal traffic. Name it Bots.
  3. Set the parameter value to bot, the same word your snippet uses.
  4. Set the state to Testing and save.

In Testing, GA4 keeps every event but marks the matching ones with a dimension called Test data filter name (source). Nothing is lost yet.

Step 3: check, then switch it on

Wait a few days. Then go back to your exploration and add Test data filter name as a dimension.

  • Rows marked Bots should look like bots: no engagement, one page, the odd screen size.
  • The unmarked rows should look like people: several pages, real time on page, search and referral traffic.

If real-looking sessions are marked, narrow the rule in your snippet. When the split looks right, set the filter to Active. A property can have up to 10 data filters.

What I learned the hard way

  • Your numbers drop the day you ship the filter. That's the point, but it looks like a disaster in a chart a month later. Write the date down somewhere you'll see it, like a GA4 annotation or a note next to the report.
  • Don't filter by city. Real people live in data-centre towns too. Use city to find bots, and the browser's own signals to filter them.
  • Skipping the tag is simpler, but blind. You can also not load GA4 at all when a visit looks automated. I did that on some sites. It works, but there's no Testing step and no record of what was skipped. Label first if you can.
  • Bots aren't your real problem. On new sites, clean numbers mostly showed how few people arrive. The fix for that is getting pages indexed, which is a different post.

The checklist

  1. Run the five-minute check in Explore: city, screen resolution, engagement.
  2. Write a rule from what you found: navigator.webdriver, headless user agents, the odd screen size.
  3. Set traffic_type: 'bot' in your snippet when the rule matches.
  4. Create an Internal traffic data filter for bot, in Testing.
  5. Check the Test data filter name split after a few days.
  6. Switch it to Active, and note the date.

entry.title: Before you fix your SEO, check that Google can see your site
entry.summary: A new site with no visitors is usually not a ranking problem. It is an indexing problem. How to check in five minutes, and what to do about it.
entry.content:
A few weeks ago I helped launch a handful of new websites. Good content, clean markup, fast pages. A week later, nobody was visiting.

So I did what most people do. I improved the pages. Better headings. More structured data. Tighter answers to the questions people search for.

None of it mattered. When I finally checked, Google had not indexed a single page. You can't rank a page a search engine has never seen.

If your new site is quiet, run these checks before you change a word on it.

If you'd rather not type the links by hand, this free checklist builder takes your domain and fills in every check below for you. It runs in your browser and sends nothing anywhere.

1. Ask Google what it knows

Search for this, with your own domain:

site:yourdomain.com

Zero results means you don't have an SEO problem yet. You have an indexing problem, and it's a much easier one to fix.

A handful of results on a site with hundreds of pages means the same thing, just smaller.

Treat the count as a rough sign, not a measurement. Google says site: doesn't necessarily return every indexed URL. For a yes or no on one page, use URL Inspection in Search Console (step 3).

2. Make sure the site isn't telling Google to stay away

This is the most common reason a finished site never shows up, and it takes two minutes to rule out. There are two ways a site can say "don't index me", often left over from when it was being built.

A noindex tag. Open your home page, right-click, choose View Page Source, and search for noindex. If you find <meta name="robots" content="noindex, Google will drop that page from its results. content="none" does the same: Google's robots meta tag reference says it's "Equivalent to noindex, nofollow". From a terminal, this prints the page's robots tags:

curl -sL https://yourdomain.com/ | grep -ioE '<meta[^>]*name=.?(robots|googlebot)[^>]*>'

That works on a Mac or Linux. The L matters: if your domain redirects, say to its www version, curl without it reads only the empty redirect and prints nothing, which looks like a pass. Look for noindex, or none on its own; index, follow or no output at all is fine. In Windows PowerShell, curl.exe -sL https://yourdomain.com/ | Select-String noindex prints any line with the word in it; check it sits inside a robots tag, not in a script or a plugin's name.

On WordPress, the usual cause is one checkbox: Settings → Reading → Search engine visibility → "Discourage search engines from indexing this site". When it's ticked, WordPress adds that noindex tag to every page. Untick it and save. Other site builders have a similar "hide from search engines" switch in their SEO or site settings, worth a look too.

A robots.txt that blocks everything. Open https://yourdomain.com/robots.txt. If you see Disallow: / under User-agent: *, crawlers are asked not to read any page. Delete that line unless you meant it. If the file is longer and you can't tell which rule applies to which page, paste it into my robots.txt tester: it shows, for each URL, whether Googlebot may crawl it and the exact line that decided.

One trap: don't use robots.txt to hide a page you want removed. Google has to crawl a page to see its noindex tag, and a robots.txt block stops it from ever seeing it.

3. Tell Google the site exists

Nothing links to a brand-new domain, so crawlers have no path to it. Waiting can take weeks. Telling them takes minutes.

  1. Open Google Search Console and add your domain as a Domain property.
  2. It gives you a TXT record. Add it at your DNS provider and click Verify. Leave the record in place afterwards: removing it un-verifies you. If you can't edit your DNS, choose a URL-prefix property instead: type the exact address your home page opens at (with or without www, as it really is) and verify with an HTML file, a meta tag or your Google Analytics tag (Google's guide to the two kinds).
  3. Under Sitemaps, submit https://yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml. Most site builders and static generators make one for you.
  4. Paste your most important page into URL Inspection and press Request indexing. "URL is on Google" means it can appear in results; "URL is not on Google" means it can't yet, and the Crawl section says why. Ask once: asking again doesn't speed it up.

4. Don't skip Bing

Bing is small for direct search, but its index travels further than its own results page. Several AI assistants and search tools build on it. Being missing from Bing can mean being missing from places you didn't think about.

In Bing Webmaster Tools you can import your sites straight from Search Console. It takes about a minute.

5. Ping IndexNow when pages change

IndexNow lets you tell participating search engines, Bing among them, that a URL is new or changed. Put a key file at your site's root, then send the URLs:

curl -X POST https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"host":"yourdomain.com",
       "key":"YOUR_KEY",
       "urlList":["https://yourdomain.com/new-page/"]}'

The key is any random string. The file at https://yourdomain.com/YOUR_KEY.txt contains the same string, which proves the site is yours.

6. Distrust your first analytics numbers

When I looked at visitor numbers for those new sites, they looked encouraging. Most of them weren't people.

They came from data-centre cities, with an 800 by 600 screen, and viewed one page. That's the fingerprint of automated crawlers and scanners. On a new site they can be most of your traffic.

Before you celebrate, or panic, filter them. Look at the city and screen-size reports. Real people come from where your customers are, on phones. I wrote up how to spot these bots in Google Analytics 4 and filter them out safely.

How long the wait is

Once the checks pass, the rest is waiting. Google's own guide says "Crawling can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks." Here is what that looked like on this site.

A daily job asks Search Console about every page in my sitemap. On 6 October, 5 of 16 pages were indexed:

  • Two pages published on 4 October were crawled and indexed the same day.
  • Two pages published on 3 October were crawled and indexed on 5 October.
  • The page you're reading, published on 2 October, was not indexed on 6 October. On 5 October Search Console said "Discovered – currently not indexed". On 6 October it said "URL is unknown to Google" again.

Two lessons from that. A status can move backwards, so one bad day isn't a verdict. And a page can wait longer than newer pages on the same site, with nothing wrong with it.

While you wait, check with URL Inspection once every few days, not every hour. If a page is still not indexed after a few weeks, go back to step 2 for that page. I keep a live record of every page on this site, updated daily, if you want to see what normal looks like.

What didn't help

Two things I tried that I'd skip next time:

  • More structured data on unindexed pages. Schema helps a page that's already in the index. On a page nobody has crawled, it's motion without movement.
  • An llms.txt file to get cited by AI. It's cheap to add and handy for developer tools. But as far as any public evidence goes, the big AI assistants don't read it when choosing what to cite. Don't count on it for visibility.

The order I use now

  1. Can search engines see it, and is it allowed to be indexed? (site: search, no stray noindex or Disallow: /, Search Console, Bing)
  2. Can they reach every page? (sitemap submitted, IndexNow on changes)
  3. Are my numbers people? (filter the bots)
  4. Only then: is the content the best answer to what someone is asking?

Step four is where the real work is. It's also the only step that doesn't matter until the first three are done.
